newsitem.title: USA: Pa. Gov. defends sale of state-run liquor stores.
newsitem.headline: Pa. Gov. defends sale of state-run liquor stores.

text.p: Pennsylvania Gov. Tom Ridge Monday defended his high-priority plan to sell off a 659 state-run liquor stores and said he would unveil a final, detailed proposal in mid-March.

Speaking at a meeting of the Pennsylvania Press Club, Ridge said the dismantling the 64-year old state liquor system, which is estimated to raise $600 million to $1 billion, would not lead to increased underage drinking, alcoholism or alcohol-related fatalities, as some critics, have charged.
Ridge has listed selling off the state stores as his top legislative priority for the new session that started in January.

The governor has proposed using money from the sale to endow a fund whose interest would be used to help Pennsylvania communities build stadiums, convention centers, aquariums, libraries and other cultural facilities.
Ridge called the formation of his plan to divest the Liquor Control Board a "work in progress."
"We have undertaken this task in a serious and responsible vein," the governor said. "It's been an ongoing process for well over four months."

Proceeds from the sale of the stores should be put toward helping the state on a long-term basis, not just for immediate gratification, Ridge said. Various groups have suggested plugging the money into the state budget to pay for such things as roads, schools and other capital assets
"The state stores are a fixed asset," he said. "To enhance their value, we'd prefer to use the proceeds as an investment in Pennsylvania's future, not to fill a budget hole on an annual basis."
The governor did not mention a specific figure for the sale proceeds, saying it depended on a variety of factors.
The national accounting firm of Price-Waterhouse is conducting a financial analysis of the sale and the Ridge administration will release its findings at the same time the plan is unveiled.

"There's a lot of speculation on the dollar amount. It depends on the nature of the plan - who sells what, when and how much," he said. "It's hard to put your arms around an actual number. I don't want to deal in unrealistic expectations. We're doing the best we can to have a fact-based approach."
Ridge denounced allegations that divesting the state stores would lead to the sale of "alcohol on every street corner," and to increased sales to teens.
Retailers and vendors who sell to minors will face harsh penalties, he added.
"I think Pennsylvanians are very conservative and responsible and their governor will present them with a conservative and very responsible plan," he said.
Alcohol education and enforcement would still remain number one priorities with the liquor system, even after divestiture, the governor said.
Pennsylvania and Utah are the only states that still directly control the distribution and sale of liquor and wine.
Ridge also attempted to allay the fears of state-store workers, whose union has vehemently opposed the sale, saying he understood their opposition and respected their work ethic.
But at the same time, he did not make any job guarantees.

"They are not the enemy. We do not propose to sell off the liquor stores because they've done anything wrong...We'll make every reasonable accommodation for them as we move toward privatization," he said.
During a question-and-answer session, Ridge said he supported imposing a toll on Interstate 80, a heavily-trafficked and costly federal highway.
Pennsylvania spends from $50 million to $60 million annually to maintain the roadway and is lobbying Washington to get permission to levy the toll, he said.
But tolling drivers on I-80 would still not generate the kind of dollars needed to improve statewide highway maintenance and build new roads.
The governor lost a battle with the Legislature last year to increase the state gas tax, but reiterated his support for the tax increase again.
--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650
